If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-7}\frac{x+7}{{x}^{2}+5x-14}=\frac{-7+7}{(-7)^{2}+5(-7)-14}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+7}{{x}^{2}+5x-14} & =\frac{x+7}{(x+7)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x+7}}{\cancel{(x+7)}(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-7}\frac{x+7}{{x}^{2}+5x-14} & ={lim}_{x\to \,-7}\frac{1}{x-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{-7-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's sketch the graph of $y=f(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14262363/assets/446f0fd704e09106f34a70fcbd3adb2806bfea13664114bd5d704fd3c8519001.png)

As $x$ decreases to $-\infty $, the graph oscillates between the values $y=-4$ and $y=4$ indefinitely. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=DNE.
$$

We have the function $f(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ Notice that we are given the length $h$ of the interval. So, the average rate of change of $f$ over this interval is given by

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

with $a=0.$ Substituting into the formula and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \\  & =\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{0}{2})}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4(1)}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4}{h} \\  & =\frac{4}{h}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph shows that as we approach $h=0$ from the left, the $y$ value approaches $0.$ So, the left-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,{0}^{-}}g(h)=0.
$$

Similarly, when we approach $h=0$ from the right, the $y$ value approaches $0.$ So, the right-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,{0}^{+}}g(h)=0.
$$

Since both the left and right-hand limits exist and are equal to $0,$ we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,0}g(h)=0.
$$

First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}\frac{1}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\frac{1}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14262363/assets/ae746b3869a36bef6740e75f1bd6c82ebf296d3a65de5860cd9dc43fc09f3c38.png)

From the graph, as $x$ approaches $\pi $ from the right, the values of $y=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{2})$ are negative and decrease without bound. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}\frac{1}{f(x)}={lim}_{x\to \,{\pi }^{+}}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=-\infty .
$$
